Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind' implies a fragmented, snapshot-like recollection, whereas 'My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed' implies a broadly coherent and detailed memory. That pair is difficult to reconcile as describing the same trauma memory without qualification, making the memory profile internally inconsistent. 'Partial Clarity' could fit with either style, but the simultaneous endorsement of both strongly snapshot-like and globally vivid/detailed memory is the main coherence problem.

vignette:
Melissa is a 38-year-old North American woman who has been working for years as a bartender, someone used to reading a room quickly, staying composed under pressure, and keeping her own reactions out of sight. She came to treatment only reluctantly, after months of putting off both medical and psychological appointments, saying that asking for help made her feel exposed and foolish. What happened had not happened to her body, but to someone she loved, and that fact sat heavily with her. She described the event in a way that was both sharply detailed and abruptly incomplete, as if some parts had been preserved in high-definition while other stretches simply dropped away.

The trauma centered on a violent injury to her partner. On the night it happened, Melissa had been with him shortly before, and she had replayed those last ordinary moments so many times that they had taken on an unbearable sharpness. She could describe specific images with startling clarity: the look on his face before they separated, the lighting, the exact visual scene when she learned something was wrong, and later the sight of him hurt. Those memories came to her mostly as pictures rather than as a full story. She said there were moments she could see “like snapshots burned in,” while other portions were blank enough that she could not place what she had done or said in between. That uneven quality unsettled her almost as much as the images themselves. She felt she should be able to account for every second, and the missing pieces became, in her mind, proof that she had failed in some crucial way.

In the weeks after the injury, Melissa became fixed on the idea that the event happened because of the way she acted. She did not present this as a passing guilty thought but as something she had come to believe about herself. If she had insisted on something different, if she had noticed more, if she had not handled that evening the way she did, then maybe the person she loved would not have been harmed. She spoke about this with the tense certainty of someone reviewing evidence in a case that was already closed against her. Alongside that self-blame was a hardening view of other people. She no longer felt that people were what they seemed. She found herself watching for hidden motives and broken promises, convinced that others could not really be relied on when it mattered.

That outlook came with her into work. Behind the bar, she was constantly surrounded by strangers who appeared friendly, affectionate, or generous and then changed within minutes after a few drinks. Even before treatment, bartending had required vigilance, but now it felt personal. A customer laughing too loudly with a companion, a sudden shift in tone between people, or fragments of conversation about someone getting hurt could make her chest tighten. She did not describe these moments in diagnostic language; instead, she said she felt herself bracing, scanning faces, trying to judge who was real and who was not. In a setting built on sociability, she became more closed off. She still did her job, but she trusted no one easily, and if coworkers offered support she dismissed it internally, certain that when things became serious, people would disappear or disappoint.

Melissa worked hard to control her emotions, especially in public. She took pride in not crying at work, not letting her voice shake, not giving customers or coworkers anything they could read. At home she tried just as forcefully to contain herself. If she felt grief, fear, or anger rising, she would clamp down on it, go silent, or busy herself with practical tasks. She avoided news reports about violence or injuries to loved ones because even a brief segment could pull up the same stark mental pictures she carried from that night. She had learned to switch channels, scroll past headlines, leave the room, or ask others not to mention certain stories. Over time, this narrowed her world. She became less informed, less willing to engage in ordinary conversations about current events, and more cut off from other people’s attempts to connect.

She also avoided seeking help. Medical settings and psychological care both felt intolerable to her, not only because they brought her close to what had happened, but because relying on professionals felt like another form of dependence she did not trust. She delayed appointments, minimized her distress, and told herself she should be able to handle it alone. What finally brought her in was not a single dramatic collapse but the accumulation of strain: the exhausting effort of staying controlled, the persistent return of vivid visual memories, the blanks in her recollection that she could not stop circling, and the growing impact on her relationship and work. By the time she sought treatment, Melissa was frightened of what it meant that this event still lived in her in fragments and images, and she was equally afraid that if she let herself depend on anyone now, she would be proven right yet again that people cannot be counted on. At the same time, she held a quieter hope that speaking about it might loosen the grip of those frozen moments and help her live with less constant guardedness.
